the domed city of the Moon, under glass in the Sea of Tranquillity
A city under a great glass dome on the grey plain, Earth hanging blue in the black sky above it. The Grand Concourse runs north to the Hall of the Lunar Compact on its terraces.

The Exchange buys what is mined in the Helium Fields and sells the city's own goods.

The first dome went up beside Tranquillity Outpost when the settlers learned to sinter moon dust into brick. Each ring of the dome was raised by the Regolith Builders, and the city grew until it filled the crater floor.
Every settlement on the Moon sends a delegate to the Compact, which meets in the Hall on the terraces. It shares out water and air first, and argues about everything else after.
The Moon has no air to breathe and none to block the Sun's harshest light. The glass of the dome is thick, layered and backed by water, so the city is safe under it.
Out through the Shackleton Tube lie the mines. Ilmenite sand gives oxygen when it is heated with hydrogen; the polar ice gives water; and helium-3, rare on Earth, lies in the dust.
Twelve people walked on the Moon between 1969 and 1972, on the Apollo missions. With no wind or rain, their footprints are still there.
From the near side, Earth never rises or sets: it hangs in nearly the same place in the sky, going through phases like the Moon does from Earth.
The Moon's gravity is about one sixth of Earth's, 1.62 metres per second squared. A person who can jump half a metre on Earth can jump about three metres here.
How strong is the Moon's gravity, compared with Earth's?
Ilmenite is a mineral of iron, titanium and oxygen. Heated with hydrogen, it gives up its oxygen as water, which can be split into oxygen to breathe and hydrogen to use again.
What can be made from ilmenite?
Near the Moon's poles are craters whose floors the Sun never reaches. They stay far below freezing, and spacecraft have found signs of water ice there.
Where is the Moon's ice found?
In craters the Sun never reaches
The Moon has almost no air, so nothing scatters sunlight across the sky. Even at midday the sky is black and the stars are there; the Sun's glare just makes them hard to see.
Why is the Moon's sky black by day?
There is almost no air to scatter light
The Moon turns once on its axis for every trip round Earth, so it always shows us the same face. We call this tidal locking.
Why do we always see the same side of the Moon?
Mare Haven is a domed city on the Moon, run by the Lunar Compact, a council of the Moon's settlements; the Space Corp keeps watch there. Real lunar science is welcome.
the red city of Mars, terraced into the crater wall above the old river delta
Under a ribbed dome on the butterscotch plain, the red stone city climbs on terraces to the Citadel of the Settlers' Assembly. The canal of melted ice runs down the Avenue of the Delta.

The Red Bazaar buys what the Delta Works bring in and sells the city's goods.
The first settlers came down beside the old river delta, where water once ran. They cut their homes into the crater wall for shelter from radiation, then raised the domes over the terraces.
Every settler has a voice in the Assembly. It meets in the Citadel at the top of the terraces, and its first duty is the water.
Martian dust storms can grow to cover the whole planet. The Dust Watch reads the sky and warns the city to close its vents.
Ice brought by convoy from the northern slopes is melted and runs down the Avenue of the Delta in a stone channel before it is cleaned and stored.
Jezero Crater held a lake about 3.5 billion years ago. NASA's Perseverance rover has explored its delta since 2021, collecting rock samples.
On Mars the sky is butterscotch by day, but sunsets are blue: the fine dust scatters blue light near the Sun.
A Martian day, called a sol, is 24 hours and 37 minutes: almost the same as Earth's. A Martian year is 687 Earth days.
How long is a sol, a day on Mars?
Mars's dust is rich in iron oxide, rust. Fine red dust blown about in the thin air coats everything and tints the sky.
The air of Mars is about 95% carbon dioxide. In 2021 the MOXIE experiment aboard Perseverance made oxygen from it, splitting carbon dioxide at about 800 degrees Celsius.
